title: Expressions from Alice in Wonderland (part 2)

image.attribution: Charles Robinson / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain.

main_content:
This article is divided in 2 parts! In part 1 we discussed the expressions that became popular through Lewis Carroll’s book “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.” In the beginning of the story Alice chases a White rabbit and falls down the rabbit hole.

Later in the story, Alice is the guest at a tea party – a crazy tea party! There she meets the March Hare and the Hatter.

As with many expressions found in Carroll’s books mad as a March hare appeared in other places long before the publication of his book.

Hares have long been thought to behave excitedly in March. Scientifically, this may not be true. But to be mad as a March hare means that someone is mad, or crazy.

The expression mad as a Hatter also means to be crazy.

Smiling like the Cheshire Cat was a common expression during Victorian times. Carroll brought this expression to life in his book with the character the Cheshire Cat. A person who is compared to the Cheshire Cat is sneaky and mysterious.

Near the end of the story, Alice meets the Queen of Hearts.

The Queen of Hearts is quick to give the death sentence by yelling, “Off with their heads! Off with their heads!”

Using expressions from popular books can add a special flavor to your English. So, have fun with them!

questions.question: Who did Alice meet at the tea party?
options: The Mad Hatter and the Queen of Hearts
The March Hare and the Hatter
The Cheshire Cat and the March Hare
The White Rabbit and the Mad Hatter
questions.answer: The March Hare and the Hatter
